text: You've already built this exact orders.csv dataset by hand with csv.DictReader back in Chapter 3 — the missing name on order 1005, the negative quantity on 1014. Pandas is how you actually clean and analyze data like this at scale, instead of writing row-by-row loops.

A Series looks like a list, but every value carries a label — the index — not just a position. Here pandas assigns the default 0, 1, 2, 3, but an index can be anything: order IDs, dates, customer names. And unlike a plain list, every value in a Series shares one dtype — here, float64.

A DataFrame is a 2-D table — rows and columns — where each column is its own Series with its own dtype, all sharing one row index. This is exactly where Chapter 3's list of dicts was always heading: a DataFrame gives you filtering, sorting, and aggregation for free.

pd.read_csv hands you a ready-to-use DataFrame with types already inferred. df.shape is rows by columns — 20 orders, 10 columns. Notice pandas inferred quantity as a real int64, but it didn't complain about order 1014's negative -1 — pandas infers type, not correctness.
df.head of 3 gives you a quick, safe peek at the start of the dataset before you commit to processing all twenty rows — the same instinct as a readline loop, just built in.
This same df is what the rest of the chapter builds on. Next up: loading it more carefully with parse_dates, plus reading the same data back from JSON and Excel.
